meeting.title: Loop Returns implementation kickoff
meeting.summary: Kickoff with Loop Returns. Snowflake plus dbt Cloud, currently reporting out of Tableau workbooks the merchants team doesn't trust because numbers drift between workbooks. Primary goal is a single governed source of truth for merchant retention and refund metrics, with self-serve exploration for the merchant success team. Dana sponsors; Marcus is hands-on with dbt.
action_items: Marcus to provision the Snowflake read-only service account against the ANALYTICS database
Marcus to invite Vector's GitHub app to the dbt repo
Sam to send the semantic layer workshop agenda for next week
Dana to nominate 3 pilot users from the merchant success team
key_decisions: Success metric for the project: merchant success team self-serves weekly reporting without analyst involvement
Refund and retention metric definitions must be signed off by finance before dashboards ship
meeting.notes: The trust problem is the story here: three Tableau workbooks compute refund rate three different ways. Finance sign-off on definitions is a hard requirement from Dana.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Thanks for making time, both. Dana, you said something in the sales cycle that stuck with me — 'we have three versions of refund rate and they're all wrong'. Start there?

transcript.speaker: Dana Whitmore
transcript.text: Ha, painfully accurate. Three Tableau workbooks, three different refund rate calculations, and the merchant success team has stopped trusting all of them. Every QBR starts with an argument about whose number is right.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Oyelaran
transcript.text: The dbt side is actually solid — fct_orders and fct_returns are well tested. The drift happens downstream where each workbook re-implements the logic on top.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Which is exactly what a semantic layer kills. Define refund rate once in the dbt project, every surface reads the same definition. That's the core of what we'll build in week one and two.

transcript.speaker: Dana Whitmore
transcript.text: One hard requirement: finance signs off on the definitions before anything ships to the merchant success team. I'm not relitigating refund rate a fourth time.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Completely reasonable — we'll build the sign-off into the plan as an explicit gate. Marcus, on access: read-only Snowflake service account and repo access for our GitHub app.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Oyelaran
transcript.text: Both easy. I'll do the service account against the ANALYTICS database today and the GitHub invite right after this call.

transcript.speaker: Caroline Jaworsky
transcript.text: That would make you the fastest-provisioning customer this quarter, for the record.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Dana, for the pilot — who actually explores data day-to-day on the merchant success side?

transcript.speaker: Dana Whitmore
transcript.text: I'll nominate three of the senior MS folks. If they can answer their own retention questions without filing an analyst ticket, this project pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: That's our success metric then — MS self-serves weekly reporting, zero analyst tickets. Sam will send the semantic layer workshop agenda; proposing Wednesdays for the weekly sync.

transcript.speaker: Dana Whitmore
transcript.text: Wednesdays work. Good energy on this one — let's keep it.

transcript.speaker: You
transcript.text: Recap and actions in your inbox shortly. Thanks all.
